findings.title: Device is cached as tagged before the limit check, so a rejected device gets in on its next request
findings.body: tagDeviceUI sets the local cache entry (`a.localCache.SetDefault(key, ...)`) before calling `CreateOrUpdateDevice`. If that call returns ErrDeviceLimitReached, the device stays cached for about 29 minutes. The next request for that device hits the cache check at the top of tagDeviceUI, returns nil, and Authenticate lets the anonymous login through without the device ever being stored. The device limit can therefore be bypassed. The cache entry should be set only after a successful store, or removed when the store returns an error.

findings.title: Count-then-insert device limit check is racy and can exceed the limit
findings.body: CreateOrUpdateDevice counts devices with CountDevices and then inserts in a separate statement. Concurrent first-time requests from different devices can all read a count below the limit and all insert, so the number of devices can overshoot deviceLimit. The check and insert need to be atomic, for example a conditional INSERT ... SELECT with a count subquery under a transaction or lock, or the limit should be documented as approximate.

findings.title: Existing devices older than the window are reported as limit-reached
findings.body: When the limit is hit, updateDevice only updates rows whose updated_at lies in [now-30d, now+1min]. An existing device whose record is older than 30 days matches no row, so rowsAffected is 0 and the function returns ErrDeviceLimitReached. That user is then rejected even though the device is already known and the limit was not exceeded for it. Also, on MySQL RowsAffected counts changed rows, so an update that changes nothing would also be misreported. The function should distinguish a missing row from an unchanged one.

findings.title: Device tagging moved from a background goroutine to the request path, adding DB work to every anonymous login
findings.body: The previous code tagged the device asynchronously with a 2-minute timeout and panic recovery. The new code calls TagDevice synchronously with the request context. Every uncached anonymous request now runs a COUNT query over anon_device and then an insert or update before login completes, so DB latency or contention directly slows authentication. The removal of the timeout and recover also means a slow DB can block the request until the client gives up.

findings.title: Constructor signature change may break dependency wiring
findings.body: ProvideAnonymousDeviceService now takes db.DB instead of anonstore.AnonStore and builds the store internally. If the wire provider set (or any other caller) still provides an anonstore.AnonStore, wire generation or compilation will fail, or the store will be built twice with different configurations. The wire definitions should be checked and regenerated to match.

findings.title: Device-limit tests don't cover the update path or the bypass case
findings.body: TestIntegrationBeyondDeviceLimit only checks that a new device is rejected at the limit. It does not check that an already-known device is still allowed to update when the limit is reached, which is the main purpose of updateDevice. It also doesn't check that a rejected device is not treated as tagged on a later request (the cache bypass), and it doesn't cover the limit being 0 with concurrent inserts. The new branch of the logic is therefore largely untested.
